Russia used the diplomatic cover to launch 76+ relentless attacks on Ukraine’s power grid, while Washington pressured Kyiv and waived Graham Act tariffs on Russian energy.

Following a unilateral U.S. energy ceasefire announcement and sanctions waiver to curb diesel prices, Russia escalated bombing campaigns against Ukraine's power generation infrastructure.

Sacrificing Ukrainian civilian infrastructure to appease global oil markets creates a perverse incentive structure that rewards relentless military aggression.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing economic convenience (WHAT) with diplomatic resolution (WHO) treats civilian blackouts as acceptable collateral damage for domestic fuel prices.

Social Physics Analysis:
The U.S. executed a smart selfish maneuver, deploying a manufactured energy crisis pretext to lift sanctions, while Russia exploited the diplomatic vacuum to terrorize civilians.

The Unavoidable Truth: Appeasing aggressors with sanctions relief while civilians freeze invites deeper war.

The Unavoidable Lie: Unilateral truces halt attacks without mutual enforcement.

Diplomatic theater that ignores ongoing infrastructure destruction is active complicity. Punishing the victim to appease oil markets inverts basic justice.

Families huddling in freezing dark while politicians haggle over oil futures represent a heartbreaking human cost. Every blackout shatters another innocent life.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Zelensky reveals how many Russian attacks have followed Trump's energy ceasefire

=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: Zelensky reveals how many Russian attacks have followed Trump's energy ceasefire ===

[Source 1 — kyivindependent.com] (URL: https://kyivindependent.com/zelensky-tells-trump-russia-keeps-violating-his-energy-ceasefire/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Zelensky reveals how many Russian attacks have followed Trump's energy ceasefire

"Tens of thousands of families are without power," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

Actual Article Body:
Help rescue animals from the front line — shop our Companion Collection 🐾

Russia has attacked Ukrainian energy and oil and gas facilities 76 times since U.S. President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between the two countries, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 18.

The attacks have continued despite Trump's announcement, as the U.S. president has so far avoided confronting Russian President Vladimir Putin over the violations while pressuring Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities, claiming they are driving up global oil prices.

"Tens of thousands of families are without power," Zelensky said.

"The Russians are trying to cause a blackout... And the U.S. needs to see that Russia is not making any concessions in response to the lifting of sanctions or agreements."

"It is Russia that must face pressure to give peace a chance," he added.

Trump unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11 without specifying its scope, taking Ukrainian officials by surprise.

Zelensky has said Ukraine is ready to adhere to a comprehensive energy truce, provided Russia does the same. He also noted that Ukrainian forces had refrained from attacking Russian refineries for several consecutive days following Trump's announcement.

Russian attacks on Ukraine's power grid have nevertheless continued, while the Kremlin has declined to make any commitments to the proposed truce.

Despite the continued strikes, Trump has declined to blame Moscow for violating the ceasefire while increasing pressure on Kyiv. His administration has threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and military aid unless Ukraine halts its attacks.

Ukraine has targeted Russian energy facilities and export infrastructure to disrupt a key source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to deprive civilians of electricity and heating.

The Kremlin said Oct. 14 the scope of Trump's energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine had not been specified, as Russian attacks on Ukraine's power grid continued.

Reporter

Tim Zadorozhnyy is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent covering foreign policy, U.S.-Ukraine relations, and political developments across Europe and Russia. He studied International Relations and European Studies at Lazarski University and Coventry University. Tim began his journalism career in Odesa in 2022 as a reporter for a local television channel. He later spent a year and a half at the Belarusian independent media outlet NEXTA, first as a news anchor and later as a managing editor. He is fluent in English, Ukrainian, and Russian.

St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed the attack, reporting fires at the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky District.

The attackers attempted to set fire to satellite antennas and a control unit, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said.

Russian strikes hit 20 locations, while falling debris was reported at four other sites.

"Tens of thousands of families are without power," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

"If it just passes through the country, then obviously there is no obstacle to it," Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said.

The number includes 2,090 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.

"I think the President wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," said Rubio.

The Lutsk facility in northwestern Ukraine, which manufactures wiring systems for BMW, Audi, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, and Skoda vehicles, was attacked by Russian drones on Oct. 16.

The two drones were jet-powered, belonging to the Geran-family of attack drones frequently used by Russia to attack targets in Ukraine, according to Romania's Defense Ministry. The Ministry did not specify which nation the drones belonged to.

Ukraine's State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko has separately reported that equipment based in Belarus helps relay or amplify signals for Russian Shahed and Geran drones heading toward western Ukraine and Poland's border region.

Among the drones it produces are the Sarych, which uses video and thermal imaging equipment for surveillance, and the Klin, a loitering munition designed to strike targets, according to Ukraine's military intelligence agency.

The Russian soldiers are believed to belong to the 38th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade, which is operating in the area. Kravchuk alleged that orders of this nature within the brigade are issued at the initiative of its commander, Colonel Valery Kazak.

"Today, this is fully under Europe's control. That means (Russian assets) are safe for now," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

Ukraine has secured contracts and assurances from partners on additional supplies of F-16 ammunition, Zelensky noted, adding that the current deliveries were at a "satisfactory level."

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Trump Throws Lifeline To Russian Energy Buyers Days Before Lindsey Graham-Backed Sanctions Take Effect

‘an important and truly historic moment’

Actual Article Body:
(Photo by Steffen Kugler /BPA via Getty Images)

President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday intending to waive multiple sanctions on Russian energy importers amid a push to lower diesel prices.

The waiver nullifies the recently signed Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act’s 100% tariff on the five largest importers of Russian fossil fuels before the law — named after the late Republican South Carolina senator and Trump ally who died suddenly in July — takes effect Sunday. The move, which provides notice to Congress, follows Trump announcing Oct. 9 an agreement with Russia to import millions of diesel barrels into U.S. and global markets amid a spike in global fuel prices. (RELATED: Senate Passes Lindsey Graham’s Neocon-Backed Bill Targeting Russia)

The order also waived the Graham Act’s 500% tariffs on Russian goods until senior Trump administration officials “determine that further action is appropriate” as they monitor countries that import Russian energy or evade U.S. sanctions.

“President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end,” White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told the Daily Caller News Foundation. “As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution. Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests.”

A White House official also said in a statement obtained by the DCNF that the president “welcomes this historic tariff and sanctions authority, passed with overwhelming bipartisan support, that also gives him the necessary flexibility and negotiating power needed to negotiate a peace deal” and “has submitted to Congress certifications and a report that these waivers are in the national interests of the United States.”

Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy of Russian President Vladimir Putin, praised the waiver in an X post Saturday.

“The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment,” Dmitriev wrote. “Economic cooperation between Russia and the United States serves the interests of both nations, contributes to global economic stability, and lays the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace.”

The US-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue. 🕊️ Some thoughts on suspending some provisions of the Graham Act 👇 https://t.co/lzjwdwFzxJ

The national average price of a barrel of diesel was $6.33 at the time of writing, up from the 2025 average of $3.64, according to AAA.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, however, criticized the waiver in an X post Saturday.

“At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end,” Zelenskyy wrote. “This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”

Yesterday, the Russians carried out one of their largest attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector – more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine. Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved. I thank everyone working practically nonstop to restore power. The most difficult situation was in Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Shepetivka, Slavuta, and Netishyn. Energy facilities in the Kharkiv, Kyiv, Dnipro, and other regions were also hit. The Russians have scaled up their anti-energy operation and are trying to stretch our reserves and repair capabilities as thin as possible. Between 7 p.m. yesterday and 7 a.m. today alone, more than 320 jet-powered and gasoline-powered “shaheds,” along with loitering munitions, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles, were used against our energy sector, our cities, and our communities. And although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them, the sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences. It is important that our European partners have already prepared new support packages for Ukraine. I am grateful to them for this. And it is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening. At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end. This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters. Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this. A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground. We must keep trying to end the war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely. I thank everyone who is truly fighting for peace and helping Ukraine!

Trump’s waiver comes after he criticized Zelenskyy for targeting Russian fuel refineries during the Russo-Ukrainian War. (RELATED: ‘It’s Time For Ukraine To Get A New President’: Trump Signals End Of Patience With Zelenskyy As War Stretches On)

“We said, ‘You can do whatever you want to Russia, [but] don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused,’” Trump told reporters Oct. 10. “And he wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmer, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world.”

“Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” Republican South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the bill’s namesake, told reporters Saturday. “Because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia.”

The U.S. Trade Representative’s office and Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to the DCNF’s requests for comment.

Editor’s note: This report was updated with comments from the White House and Sen. Graham.
